summary: Stella Protocol is an interactive strategy and real-world problem-solving video game inspired by the hazards of NASA spaceflight. Featuring a striking visual interface, players command the spacecraft Astraea on a journey to the Moon, Mars, and Jupiter, managing budgets, engineering design, environmental testing, and a specialized crew. When communication with Earth is lost, users must navigate real-world crises involving microgravity, isolation, and mechanical failures across 10 turns recorded in an illustrated logbook. By transforming complex scientific concepts into an engaging and educational experience, the game helps foster and cultivate a passion for space-tech fields among new generations.
details:
What it does and how it works

Stella Protocol is a free browser game where you become NASA's Flight Director.

The game has seven phases:

Destination: the Moon's south pole, Mars or Europa. Each has its own budget, distance, sunlight, signal delay and radiation.

Crew: four astronauts with different roles and command styles.

Design: you build a spacecraft (power, propulsion, comms, instruments, life support, shielding and exploration vehicles) within a real budget and launcher mass limit.

Flight Readiness Review: seven Mission Control consoles vote GO or NO-GO, with a 5×5 risk matrix.

Launch: a cinematic launch with staging and orbit insertion.

Mission: a day-by-day logbook. You assign each astronaut a job, manage oxygen, water, food and power, and repair failing systems. You also choose where the rover drives on a map of real sites and react to events based on real NASA history.

Legacy: endings, crew epilogues and the real lesson NASA learned from each kind of failure.

A simulation runs underneath. It tracks each astronaut's health, energy and morale, plus radiation dose and five ship systems that wear out and can fail. About 40 events change their odds depending on your destination, your design and your commander. Every event shows the real fact behind it, such as Apollo 13's improvised CO₂ filter, Spirit stuck in Martian sand or Ingenuity's 72 flights.

Benefits

The game turns NASA's engineering mindset into decisions with visible consequences: keeping margins, avoiding single points of failure, respecting the GO/NO-GO process and protecting the crew from the five hazards of human spaceflight. It works on any computer or phone with nothing to install, and it is available in English and Spanish.

Expected impact

We want students and the general public to understand why space missions are designed the way they are. Mission design is a chain of trade-offs: mass against shielding, science against safety, schedule against crew health. When a mission fails, the player learns the real lesson NASA learned from a similar failure, so even losing teaches something. Teachers can use it in class as a short, hands-on introduction to systems engineering and space exploration.

Tools, languages and software

Languages and libraries: JavaScript, React 19, Vite, Three.js with React Three Fiber and Drei for 3D, zustand for game state, and the Web Audio API for sound.

3D: Blender 5.3 to model the astronauts (using a reference image generated with Google Gemini) and the ship, and to lighten NASA's official 3D models (Perseverance, Ingenuity, Apollo Lunar Module) for the web.

NASA data: planet textures from NASA SVS, USGS and JPL.

Testing: oxlint, about 87,000 automated checks (including thousands of simulated missions) and a browser test.

Hosting: Vercel.

AI: Anthropic's Claude helped write code and text under the team's direction, and Google Gemini generated a reference image for the astronauts, which the team then modelled in Blender. The team reviewed every feature and fact-checked the facts shown to players against NASA sources.

Why it is creative

Logbook interface: instead of a dashboard, the mission is a hand-drawn logbook, which makes the player feel like a real flight director.

Visible consequences: in the 3D ship, the crew walks to their jobs, failures flash red, and on the surface the rover drives across sites with real names.

"Classified files": rare events built on popular myths (the Face on Mars, the Black Knight satellite, the Wow! signal), where investigating reveals the scientific explanation.

Original sound: the music and sound effects are synthesized live in code, with no audio files.

What our team considered

Accuracy: every event and lesson is based on NASA sources, such as the Human Research Program, the Systems Engineering Handbook and mission records.

Accessibility: the game runs in a browser, adapts graphics quality to the device and works on phones.

Learning through play: each choice teaches a real concept without long lectures, and a short tutorial explains the basics.

Respect for the data and credits: we used only public-domain NASA resources and did not use the NASA logo. We credited every external resource, including the AI tools we used and the Pinterest design that inspired our home screen.
